newsitem.title: USA: Police surround armed separatists in Texas standoff.
newsitem.headline: Police surround armed separatists in Texas standoff.

text.p: FBI agents and police surrounded armed separatists at a fortified compound in west Texas on Monday weighing whether to move in and arrest the group's leader or negotiate an end to the tense standoff.

The "Republic of Texas" separatists freed two hostages overnight but officials said they were still concerned about the safety of dozens of local residents trapped in their homes by the standoff and police reinforcements moved into the area.

"We are still considering this a hostage situation because there are between 90 and 150 people in there that cannot come and go because the Republic of Texas has that road blocked," Sherri Deatherage-Green, a Texas Department of Public Safety spokeswoman said.

The group and its self-designated ambassador, Richard McLaren, have been holed up inside their compound for the last four months in a resort community deep in the remote Davis Mountains of southwest Texas.

The group's security chief, Bob Scheidt, was arrested on weapons possession charges early on Sunday so McLaren ordered a Republic unit to attack the nearby home of a middle-aged couple, Joe and Margaret Rowe, and take them hostage.

After 12 hours of negotiations the Rowes were released in exchange for the return of Scheidt to the group's compound. Joe Rowe, a bitter critic of the Republic's leaders, was shot during the raid on his home but received medical attention imemdiately after his release and was in fair condition.

Although the prisoner exchange eased tension in the area, police refused to back off and were still mulling their options early on Monday. An arrest warrant was issued for Mclaren last December but he refuses to surrender and warns any raid on his compound would be repelled.

It was not clear how many men were inside the compound or how heavily they were armed. But federal officials, mindful of the disastrous conclusion to similar standoffs at Ruby Ridge, Idaho and the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, are wary of sparking any violent clash.

McLaren said thousands of his "defense force" troops and allied militia members would rush to his defence if police tried to arrest him, but officials dispute those claims and so far there has been no sign of any such mobilisation.

FBI and police units closed off roads leading to the Republic compound, which was once a volunteer firehouse, and its telephone line was disconnected to prevent McLaren from speaking with media or outside supporters.

State officials said continuing negotiations with the group focused on guaranteeing the safety of local residents. About 150 people are permanent residents of the Fort Davis Resort subdivision where the compound is located and scores more have homes there.

Republic leaders claim Texas' 1845 annexation into the United States was unconstitutional and demand that the Lone Star state be recognised as a soveriegn nation with themselves as its provisional leaders. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke away from Mexico in 1836.
The Republic group emerged in 1995, set up its own court system and militia units, and has since filed thousands of liens against government agencies and private property owners.

State officials said the liens are bogus and are aimed at clogging up the state's courts. They also accuse the group of using millions of dollars of fraudulent but official looking checks made out in the name of the Republic of Texas.

McLaren said the group's actions are legitimate because its courts last year issued a $93 trillion lien against the U.S. government, the United Nations and the Roman Catholic Church for allegedly plundering Texas' wealth over 150 years.
McLaren was charged with contempt of court last December for failing to appear in a federal court in nearby Pecos on charges related to the liens.
